query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Polycrystalline FCC copper exhibits high ductility under ambient quasi‐static loading because its crystal structure contains multiple {111} slip systems and a low stacking fault energy that facilitates efficient dislocation nucleation and glide.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline face-centered cubic (FCC) copper at ambient temperature and pressure.
generation.intervention: Perform molecular dynamics simulations that systematically vary the stacking fault energy and explore different grain boundary structures.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature and pressure under quasi‐static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsic FCC crystal structure, characterized by abundant {111} slip planes and typical grain boundary configurations.
generation.mechanism: The low stacking fault energy in FCC copper enables the nucleation and propagation of dislocations along multiple {111} slip systems, which allows for plastic deformation to occur without premature fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Copper samples with favorable stacking fault characteristics are expected to display increased ductile strain and sustained plastic deformation, evidenced by a higher density of dislocations propagating on the {111} planes compared to modifications that impede these processes.
generation.baseline: Standard polycrystalline copper with its inherent stacking fault energy and grain structure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is specifically applicable to conventional FCC metals under ambient quasi‐static loading; it may not extend to non‐FCC materials or conditions involving extreme temperatures or very high strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative sensitivity of ductility to changes in stacking fault energy and grain boundary structure is not fully defined, and further simulation work is needed to establish precise thresholds.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and simulate several polycrystalline FCC copper samples under ambient, quasi‐static conditions using molecular dynamics. Systematically vary the stacking fault energy and modify the grain boundary structures in silico. Measure the onset and propagation of dislocation activity along the {111} planes and record the overall ductile strain prior to failure.
measurements: Dislocation density and propagation patterns on {111} slip systems
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If modification of the stacking fault energy and grain boundary character does not result in consistent and reproducible changes in dislocation behavior and measurable ductile strain relative to the baseline polycrystalline copper, then the hypothesis—that these features are key to the enhanced ductility of FCC copper—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloys has progressively focused on deciphering the underlying factors that enable high ductility. Some studies (for example, PMC6093928 on the Cantor alloy) have used density‐functional simulations to relate parameters like stacking fault energy and dislocation behavior to a material’s ability to plastically deform. Other papers have tackled ductility indirectly by tuning microstructures via advanced processing methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering, thermo‐mechanical treatments) that lead to multiphase or coherent precipitate architectures, demonstrating that the activation of multiple slip systems is crucial. However, while these studies have advanced alloy design strategies—especially in complex HEAs—the direct analysis of why an FCC metal (such as copper or aluminum, which naturally feature many available slip systems and inherently low stacking fault energies) exhibits excellent ductility under ambient conditions remains less explored.
decision.unsolved: A systematic, atomistic-level understanding linking the intrinsic crystal structure of traditional FCC metals (e.g., copper or aluminum) to their ductile behavior under relevant loading conditions is missing. In particular, a direct simulation-based study that maps out dislocation nucleation, slip system activation, and stacking fault energetics for these basic FCC systems to rationalize their superior ductility has not yet been carried out.
decision.lever: Perform molecular dynamics simulations focused on mapping dislocation nucleation and slip on {111} planes in FCC metals (e.g., copper or aluminum) while systematically varying stacking fault energies and grain boundary structures.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend of using atomistic insights—in previously studied complex alloy systems—to isolate and quantify the key structural mechanisms that give rise to ductility. By applying similar simulation techniques to traditional FCC metals, researchers can rigorously validate the link between the intrinsic crystallographic features and ductile behavior, thereby addressing the noted gap.
